items.title: Q1 · Dec 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Postmodern & Contemporary Literature · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post World War II · Sharankumar Limbale
items.stem: Sharankumar Limbale argues that Dalit literature is unique because: (A) This brings out the Dalit reality which is liminal in time and space. (B) This has unique historical and ideological concerns. (C) This offers literary and cultural representations of marginalised and dispossessed people. (D) This brings out narratives and discourses of pity. (E) It uses disrespectful and offensive language towards revered figures. Choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: In Towards an Aesthetic of Dalit Literature (2004), Sharankumar Limbale asserts that Dalit literature is unique because it articulates the liminal lived reality of Dalits (A), addresses distinctive historical and ideological struggles against caste oppression (B), and gives voice to marginalized and dispossessed communities (C). It explicitly rejects patronizing upper-caste narratives of pity (making D false) and does not exist simply to use offensive language (making E false).

items.title: Q2 · Dec 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Romantic Period · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Edgar Allan Poe
items.stem: Edgar Allan Poe is often called as the originator of the short story as an established genre. He defined 'the prose tale' as:
options: A narrative which can be read at one sitting of from half an hour to two hours.
A narrative which can be read within five minutes or less.
A narrative that can be read at one sitting of from one hour to four hours.
A narrative that may be concluded and enjoyed in the single spell of less than half an hour.
items.explanation: In his 1842 review of Nathaniel Hawthorne's Twice-Told Tales, Edgar Allan Poe formulated his seminal theory of the short story, defining the 'prose tale' as a narrative requiring from half an hour to one or two hours in its perusal to produce a single, unified emotional effect.

items.title: Q3 · Dec 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Postmodern & Contemporary Literature · Unit II: Poetry · Kamala Das
items.stem: "An Introduction" by Kamla Das is:
options: A short story on the theme of people's rights and freedom
An introduction to her autobiography My Story
An essay on the theme of gender rights
A poem of resistance and protest
items.explanation: Kamala Das's 'An Introduction' (published in Summer in Calcutta, 1965) is a landmark confessional poem of protest and resistance against patriarchal domestic restrictions, societal policing of female desire, and linguistic colonization.

items.title: Q4 · Dec 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Postmodern & Contemporary Literature · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post World War II · Jean-Francois Lyotard, Jean Baudrillard, Fredric Jameson
items.stem: Which of the following statements/concepts are relevant for understanding of Postmodernism? (A) Postmodernism and Postcolonialism are mutually dependent in responding to colonial experience. (B) Lyotard argues that the Postmodern condition is characterised by a deeply felt scepticism towards metanarratives. (C) Edward W. Said has been instrumental in postmodern theory and criticism. (D) Jean Baudrillard's Simulacra and Simulations is a seminal postmodern text. (E) Fredric Jameson argues that parody has been replaced by pastiche in postmodernism. Choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Statements (B), (D), and (E) are central to postmodern theory: Jean-François Lyotard defined the postmodern condition as 'incredulity toward metanarratives' in 1979, Jean Baudrillard published Simulacra and Simulation in 1981, and Fredric Jameson famously argued that blank pastiche has replaced parody in late capitalism. In contrast, Edward Said is foundational to postcolonialism rather than postmodernism (C is false), and postmodernism is not inherently dependent on responding to colonial experience (A is false).

items.title: Q5 · Dec 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · Virginia Woolf
items.stem: "All writers since Chaucer have come from the middle class... have had good, at least expensive education...." Where has Virginia Woolf explained it?
items.explanation: Virginia Woolf made this observation in 'The Leaning Tower' (1940), an essay delivered as a lecture to the Workers' Educational Association in Brighton, where she argued that from Chaucer onward English literature had been created almost exclusively by the educated middle and upper classes perched atop a tower of economic privilege.

items.title: Q6 · Dec 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Victorian Period · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Charles Dickens
items.stem: What is the correct order of publication of the novels of Charles Dickens? (A) Great Expectations (B) Hard Times (C) Oliver Twist (D) David Copperfield (E) A Tale of Two Cities Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: The chronological publication order of Charles Dickens's novels is: Oliver Twist (1837-1839), David Copperfield (1849-1850), Hard Times (1854), A Tale of Two Cities (1859), and Great Expectations (1860-1861) [(C), (D), (B), (E), (A)].

items.title: Q7 · Dec 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Postmodern & Contemporary Literature · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Krishna Sobti, Saros Cowasjee, Rahi Masoom Raza
items.stem: Which among the following writers are popular for partition narratives? (A) Krishna Sobti (B) Shashi Deshpande (C) Saros Cowasjee (D) Bharti Mukherjee (E) Rahi Masoom Raza Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Krishna Sobti (author of Zindaginama and the Partition story 'Sikka Badal Gaya'), Saros Cowasjee (editor of Stories and Sketches of Pakistan and the Partition and Orphan of the Storm), and Rahi Masoom Raza (author of the acclaimed Partition novel Aadha Gaon / Half a Village, 1966) are prominent Partition writers [(A), (C), and (E)]. In contrast, Shashi Deshpande writes feminist domestic fiction (That Long Silence) and Bharati Mukherjee writes diasporic immigrant novels (Jasmine).

items.title: Q8 · Dec 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Literary Criticism & Theory · Unit VII: Cultural Studies · Matthew Arnold, Christopher Caudwell, T. S. Eliot, Raymond Williams, Herbert Read
items.stem: Arrange the chronological sequence in which the following works were published: (A) Culture and Society (B) Culture and Anarchy (C) To Hell with Culture (D) Studies in Dying Culture (E) Notes towards the Definition of Culture Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: The correct publication chronology is Matthew Arnold's Culture and Anarchy (1869), Christopher Caudwell's Studies in a Dying Culture (1938), T.S. Eliot's Notes towards the Definition of Culture (1948), Raymond Williams's Culture and Society (1958), and Herbert Read's To Hell with Culture (1963) [(B), (D), (E), (A), (C)]. Because this correct sequence was not listed among any of the four options, this question was officially dropped by NTA.

items.title: Q9 · Dec 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Postmodern & Contemporary Literature · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Toni Morrison, Chinua Achebe, Margaret Atwood, George Orwell
items.stem: Match List - I with List - II. List - I (Character) List - II (Novel) (A) Sethe (I) The Handmaid's Tale (B) Okonkwo (II) Beloved (C) Offred (III) Things Fall Apart (D) Winston Smith (IV) Nineteen Eighty-Four Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: The correct character-to-novel pairings are: Sethe is the runaway slave protagonist in Toni Morrison's Beloved (1987) [(A)-(II)]; Okonkwo is the tragic Igbo warrior in Chinua Achebe's Things Fall Apart (1958) [(B)-(III)]; Offred is the narrator-handmaid in Margaret Atwood's The Handmaid's Tale (1985) [(C)-(I)]; and Winston Smith is the dissident outer-party worker in George Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four (1949) [(D)-(IV)].

items.title: Q10 · Dec 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit V: Language: Basic Concepts, Theories and Pedagogy
items.stem: Which among the following statements are true? (A) Miscegenation is a sexual relationship or marriage between the people of the same race (B) Creole is a language that has evolved from a pidgin but serves as the native language of a speech community (C) Indian tribal people are popularly termed as aboriginals (D) Mulatto is a person of mixed white and black ancestry (E) Australian indigenous population is termed as Red Indians Choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Statements (B) and (D) are true: a creole is a pidgin that has expanded to become the native first language of a community, and 'mulatto' historically denoted a person of mixed European and African descent. Statements (A), (C), and (E) are false because miscegenation refers to sexual relations or marriage between different races (not the same race), Indian indigenous tribes are called Adivasis, and 'Red Indians' was a historical term applied to Indigenous Americans, not Australians.

items.title: Q11 · Dec 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Literary Criticism & Theory · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post World War II · Edward Said, Michel Foucault
items.stem: Which of the following is true of Edward Said's Orientalism? (A) It was published in 1979. (B) Utilises the concept of discursive formulation as argued by Foucault. (C) He has taken up the detailed analysis of imaginative geography and representation of the Orient. (D) It is one of the foundational texts of Postcolonial theory. (E) It puts to use Barthes' concept of 'death of the author'. Choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: In Orientalism (1978), Edward Said utilized Michel Foucault's concept of discursive formations (B) to analyze Western imaginative geography and colonial representations of the Orient (C), creating a foundational text of postcolonial theory (D). Statement (A) is false as it was published in 1978, and (E) is false because Said retained authorial agency and historical responsibility rather than adopting Barthes' 'death of the author'.

items.title: Q12 · Dec 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Literary Criticism & Theory · Unit VII: Cultural Studies · Raymond Williams
items.stem: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R). Assertion (A): Culture is one of the two or three most complicated words in the English language. Reason (R): This is mainly because of several different though related meanings have emerged at particular moments throughout its long history. In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A).
items.explanation: In Keywords: A Vocabulary of Culture and Society (1976), Raymond Williams opens his discussion by noting that 'culture' is one of the two or three most complicated words in English because its meaning evolved historically from agricultural tending to intellectual cultivation and finally to an entire way of life, making Reason (R) the direct historical explanation for Assertion (A).

items.title: Q13 · Dec 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit X: Research Methods and Materials in English
items.stem: Use of broader principles of research underscored by philosophical rationales is termed as:
items.explanation: Research methodology denotes the overarching philosophical framework, theoretical assumptions, and rationale that govern an investigation, whereas research methods and tools refer to the specific practical procedures and instruments used to gather data.

items.title: Q14 · Dec 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Ezra Pound
items.stem: Who among the following declared in 1920 that "there is no longer any intellectual life in England"?
items.explanation: Ezra Pound wrote this in a 1920 letter to William Carlos Williams before departing London for Paris and Italy, declaring that intellectual vitality in England had died out and that provincial conservatism had overtaken the London literary world.

items.title: Q15 · Dec 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Romantic Period · Unit II: Poetry · John Clare, Percy Bysshe Shelley
items.stem: Identify the poet of the following poems: (a) The Skylark (b) The Badger (c) The Gypsy Camp (d) First Love
items.explanation: The 19th-century Romantic peasant-poet John Clare wrote these intimate poems celebrating English wildlife and rural scenes; while P.B. Shelley wrote 'To a Skylark', John Clare composed 'The Skylark', 'The Badger', 'The Gypsy Camp', and 'First Love'.

items.title: Q16 · Dec 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Literary Criticism & Theory · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post World War II · Jean Baudrillard
items.stem: The term 'simulacra' in postmodern discourse is about: (A) Absence of vivid representation of reality (B) Artificially produced reality dubbed as authentic (C) A rejection of modernistic view of reality (D) The gap between the perception and reality (E) The psychological interplay at the level of subconscious Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: In Simulacra and Simulation (1981), Jean Baudrillard defines simulacra as copies without an original - simulated realities that lack genuine referential substance (A) yet are produced and received as authentic in hyperreal consumer culture (B).

items.title: Q17 · Dec 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Victorian Period · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Charles Dickens
items.stem: Which two cities are referred in Charles Dickens' A Tale of Two Cities?
items.explanation: Set against the violent upheaval of the French Revolution, Charles Dickens's historical novel A Tale of Two Cities (1859) explicitly contrasts London and Paris through the intertwined fates of Charles Darnay and Sydney Carton.

items.title: Q18 · Dec 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Romantic Period · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · Ralph Waldo Emerson
items.stem: Transcendental Club was a group of American intellectuals for philosophical discussions. Which text among the following is taken as a short treatise on Transcendentalism?
items.explanation: Ralph Waldo Emerson's landmark essay Nature (1836) served as the primary philosophical manifesto and short foundational treatise of American Transcendentalism, establishing its doctrine of the Over-Soul, intuition, and nature as a symbol of spirit.

items.title: Q21 · Dec 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Postmodern & Contemporary Literature · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · Doris Pilkington
items.stem: Given below are two statements: Statement (I): Non-fictional narrative Follow the Rabbit-Proof Fence by Doris Pilkington is based on the real-life experiences of three aboriginal girls who fled from the Moore River Native Settlement. Statement (II): The names of the three girls are- Molly, Daisy and Mary. In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both Statement (I) and Statement (II) are correct
Both Statement (I) and Statement (II) are incorrect
Statement (I) is correct but Statement (II) is incorrect
Statement (I) is incorrect but Statement (II) is correct
items.explanation: Statement (I) is correct because Doris Pilkington Garimara's Follow the Rabbit-Proof Fence (1996) documents the true escape of three Aboriginal girls of the Stolen Generations from the Moore River Native Settlement in 1931. Statement (II) is incorrect because the three girls were Molly, Daisy, and Gracie (not Mary).

items.title: Q22 · Dec 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Literary Criticism & Theory · Unit VII: Cultural Studies · Richard Hoggart
items.stem: Arrange the chronological sequence in which the following works of Richard Hoggart were published: (A) An Imagined Life (B) The Uses of Literacy (C) Higher Education: Demand and Response (D) A Local Habitation (E) A Sort of Clowning Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: The publication sequence of Richard Hoggart's works is: The Uses of Literacy (1957), Higher Education: Demand and Response (1980), followed by the three volumes of his autobiography: A Local Habitation (1988), A Sort of Clowning (1990), and An Imagined Life (1992) [(B), (C), (D), (E), (A)].

items.title: Q23 · Dec 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Postmodern & Contemporary Literature · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Jean Rhys, Emily Bronte, Charles Dickens, Chinua Achebe
items.stem: Match List - I with List - II. List - I (Character) List - II (Work) (A) Christophine (I) Wuthering Heights (B) Zillah (II) Wide Sargasso Sea (C) Estella (III) Things Fall Apart (D) Ekwefi (IV) Great Expectations Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: The correct character-to-work matches are: Christophine is the loyal Martinican nurse in Jean Rhys's Wide Sargasso Sea (1966) [(A)-(II)]; Zillah is the servant at Wuthering Heights in Emily Brontë's Wuthering Heights (1847) [(B)-(I)]; Estella is Miss Havisham's haughty adopted daughter in Charles Dickens's Great Expectations (1861) [(C)-(IV)]; and Ekwefi is Okonkwo's second wife in Chinua Achebe's Things Fall Apart (1958) [(D)-(III)].

items.title: Q24 · Dec 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Restoration & 18th Century · Unit I: Drama · Oliver Goldsmith
items.stem: Which of the following characteristics of She Stoops to Conquer is not correct?
options: It is endowed with an ingenious and lively plot.
It does not cast excellent characters.
It has a vivacious and delightful style.
items.explanation: Oliver Goldsmith's She Stoops to Conquer (1773) is renowned precisely for its vivid, delightful comic characters - including Tony Lumpkin, Kate Hardcastle, Charles Marlow, and Mrs. Hardcastle - making the statement that it does not cast excellent characters completely false.

items.title: Q25 · Dec 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Literary Criticism & Theory · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post World War II · Antonio Gramsci
items.stem: Antonio Gramsci's Prison Notebooks primarily deals with:
options: Pain of a prisoner during colonial times
Recollections of love, romance and blissful life
Philosophy, culture, literature and the role of intellectuals
Exploitation of blacks during the colonial times
items.explanation: Written between 1929 and 1935 during Antonio Gramsci's imprisonment by the Italian fascist state, the Prison Notebooks (Quaderni del carcere) develops foundational Marxist theories regarding cultural hegemony, civil society, historical materialism, and the socio-political role of organic and traditional intellectuals.

items.title: Q26 · Dec 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Literary Criticism & Theory · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post World War II · Virginia Woolf, Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak
items.stem: Given below are two statements: Statement (I): A Room of One's Own is a feminist essay about women's education, exclusion and writing by Virginia Woolf. Statement (II): In Other Worlds is a collection of essays written by Edward W. Said on contemporary ideas such as psychoanalysis and social theory. In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below
options: Both Statement (I) and Statement (II) are true
Both Statement (I) and Statement (II) are false
Statement (I) is true but Statement (II) is false
Statement (I) is false but Statement (II) is true
items.explanation: Statement (I) is true because Virginia Woolf's A Room of One's Own (1929) is a classic feminist essay examining women's education, financial independence, and literary tradition. Statement (II) is false because In Other Worlds: Essays in Cultural Politics (1987) was written by Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak, not Edward Said.

items.title: Q27 · Dec 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit I: Drama · Tennessee Williams
items.stem: Which of the following is true about Tennessee Williams' A Street Car Named Desire? (A) It is set in New Orleans. (B) The protagonist is a Mississippi landowner. (C) It ends with Blanche's defeat and departure. (D) Tom Wingfield is the narrator. (E) Laura and Stella are cousins. Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Tennessee Williams's A Streetcar Named Desire (1947) is set in the French Quarter of New Orleans [(A)] and concludes with Blanche DuBois's tragic mental collapse and removal to an asylum [(C)]. Statements (B), (D), and (E) are false because Stanley is a factory worker, Blanche lost the Belle Reve estate, and Tom and Laura Wingfield are characters from Williams's The Glass Menagerie.

items.title: Q28 · Dec 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Restoration & 18th Century · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Aphra Behn
items.stem: Prose romances preceded the emergence of novel as a popular literary genre. Which texts among the following fall under the category of Prose Romance?
options: The Pilgrim's Progress and The Spectator
items.explanation: Aphra Behn's Oroonoko: or, the Royal Slave (1688) and The Fair Jilt (1688) are prominent late 17th-century Restoration prose romances and novellas that combined romantic adventure with realistic narrative techniques, directly paving the way for the rise of the English novel.

items.title: Q29 · Dec 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Victorian Period · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Leo Tolstoy
items.stem: Which of the following statement(s) best describe Anna Karenina's situation and worldview? (A) Anna is deeply committed to the family and children (B) Anna's choices were more an outcome of passion and instinct (C) Anna accepted the exile to which she was condemned (D) Anna's passionate spirit and determination to live life at her own terms make her so unique (E) She became a victim of rampant patriarchal forces Choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: In Leo Tolstoy's Anna Karenina (1878), Anna is deeply devoted to her son Seryozha [(A)], lives by an uncompromising passion that rejects social hypocrisy [(D)], and ultimately becomes the tragic casualty of an unforgiving patriarchal society that excuses adulterous men while destroying fallen women [(E)]. Statement (C) is false because Anna never placidly accepts her social exile, which causes her fatal psychological torment.

items.title: Q30 · Dec 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Literary Criticism & Theory · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Allen Tate, Robert Penn Warren, R. P. Blackmur, Kenneth Burke
items.stem: Which of the following assumptions are true in the context of New Criticism? (A) The new movement in literature popularised closed reading of the text. (B) The leading critics of New Criticism are Allen Tate, Robert Penn Warren, R.P. Blackmur and Kenneth Burke. (C) The critical approach is extensively used in the study of novels and plays. (D) This critical approach tends to discredit historical, social and political contexts of a work of literature. (E) J.C. Ransom published a book New Criticism wherein he appreciates I.A. Richards, William Empson and T.S. Eliot. Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: New Criticism popularized close reading of the text as an autonomous verbal icon [(A)], counted prominent critics like Allen Tate, Robert Penn Warren, R.P. Blackmur, and Kenneth Burke among its practitioners [(B)], and deliberately minimized external historical, social, and biographical contexts [(D)]. Statement (C) is false because New Criticism applied its methods almost exclusively to lyric poetry rather than extended prose fiction or drama.

items.title: Q31 · Dec 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Literary Criticism & Theory · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post World War II · Roland Barthes
items.stem: Roland Barthes in his "Introduction to the Structural Analysis of Narratives" (1966) proposed three levels of narrative structure. Which among the following are the narrative structures proposed by him: (A) Functions (B) Actions (C) Grammar (D) Narration (E) Coherence Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: In his seminal essay 'Introduction to the Structural Analysis of Narratives' (1966), Roland Barthes identified three hierarchical levels of narrative structure: the level of functions (distributional and integrational units), the level of actions (characters as actants), and the level of narration (the narrative discourse and communication) [(A), (B), and (D)].

items.title: Q32 · Dec 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Literary Criticism & Theory · Unit VII: Cultural Studies · Raymond Williams
items.stem: Which of the following is not true about Raymond Williams' views on culture?
options: Culture is a whole way of life
The masses do not participate in the creation of cultural values
There exists at least three layers of a culture at a given point of time in a society- dominant, residual and emergent
items.explanation: In 'Culture is Ordinary' (1958) and Culture and Society (1958), Raymond Williams insisted that culture is actively made and lived by ordinary working-class people, directly refuting the elitist Leavisite claim that the masses do not participate in creating cultural values.

items.title: Q33 · Dec 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Postmodern & Contemporary Literature · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Amitav Ghosh
items.stem: The Calcutta Chromosome (1995) is a novel exploring past and future. It has been written by:
items.explanation: The Calcutta Chromosome (1995) is an acclaimed science-fiction and speculative novel by Amitav Ghosh that intertwines Sir Ronald Ross's malaria discovery with subaltern counter-science, winning the Arthur C. Clarke Award in 1997.

items.title: Q34 · Dec 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Literary Criticism & Theory · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post World War II · Frantz Fanon, Ernest Gellner, Homi K. Bhabha, Robert J. C. Young, Simon Gikandi
items.stem: Identify the correct order of the publications given below: (A) Simon Gikandi's Maps of Englishness: Writing Identity in the Culture of Colonialism (B) Frantz Fanon's The Wretched of the Earth (C) Homi K. Bhabha's Nation and Narration (D) Ernest Gellner's Nations and Nationalisms (E) Robert Young's Colonial Desire: Hybridity in Theory, Culture and Race Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: The chronological sequence of publication is: Frantz Fanon's The Wretched of the Earth (1961), Ernest Gellner's Nations and Nationalism (1983), Homi K. Bhabha's edited volume Nation and Narration (1990), Robert J.C. Young's Colonial Desire: Hybridity in Theory, Culture and Race (1995), and Simon Gikandi's Maps of Englishness (1996) [(B), (D), (C), (E), (A)].

items.title: Q35 · Dec 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Renaissance, Elizabethan & Jacobean Age · Unit I: Drama · John Heywood
items.stem: Who of the following was the immediate predecessor of the drama proper?
items.explanation: The Tudor Interlude (flourishing in the early-to-mid 16th century with playwrights like John Heywood) was a short secular dramatic piece performed at feasts or banquets that served as the immediate developmental link between medieval morality plays and Elizabethan drama proper.

items.title: Q36 · Dec 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Postmodern & Contemporary Literature · Unit I: Drama · Samuel Beckett
items.stem: Which of the following is true about Samuel Beckett's Waiting for Godot? (A) It illustrates vanity of human kind. (B) It has uncompromising views on humanitarian communism. (C) It projects self-deception, striving to disguise failure. (D) It is a static representation without structure or development. (E) Its incoherent dialogue suggests despair of a society. Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Samuel Beckett's Waiting for Godot (1953) is a seminal absurdist play that replaces conventional linear dramatic progression with a circular, static structure where nothing happens [(D)], utilizing disjointed and repetitive dialogue to mirror the post-war existential despair of modern civilization [(E)].

items.title: Q37 · Dec 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Postmodern & Contemporary Literature · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Raja Rao, R. K. Narayan, Manohar Malgonkar, Shashi Tharoor, Arundhati Roy
items.stem: What is the correct chronological order of publication of the texts given under? (A) R.K. Narayan's The Financial Expert (B) Manohar Malgonkar's A Bend in the Ganges (C) Raja Rao's Kanthapura (D) Shashi Tharoor's The Great Indian Novel (E) Arundhati Roy's The God of Small Things Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: The chronological publication sequence is: Raja Rao's Kanthapura (1938), R.K. Narayan's The Financial Expert (1952), Manohar Malgonkar's A Bend in the Ganges (1964), Shashi Tharoor's The Great Indian Novel (1989), and Arundhati Roy's The God of Small Things (1997) [(C), (A), (B), (D), (E)].

items.title: Q38 · Dec 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Literary Criticism & Theory · Unit I: Drama · Bhasa
items.stem: Who among the following is the earliest available Indian dramatist?
items.explanation: Bhasa (dating roughly to the 2nd-3rd century CE or earlier) is considered the earliest surviving classical Sanskrit playwright, whose thirteen complete plays - including Svapnavasavadattam, Urubhanga, and Karnabhara - were rediscovered in 1912 by Pandit T. Ganapati Sastri.

items.title: Q39 · Dec 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Literary Criticism & Theory · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post World War II · Ngugi wa Thiong'o, Homi K. Bhabha, Edward Said, Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak
items.stem: Which of the following statements are valid for postcolonial theory and literature? (A) Abrogation, resistance and assertion form the basis of postcolonial thought. (B) Postcolonial theory defends binaries of Master and Slave, White and Black, and Coloniser and Colonised. (C) Weep Not, Child is the first novel in English by an East African Writer, Ngugi Wa Thiong'o. (D) Wide Sargasso Sea by Jean Rhys is based on the experiences of colonized African population. (E) Homi K. Bhabha, Edward W. Said and Gayatri Spivak are important postcolonial thinkers. Choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Statements (A), (C), and (E) are valid: abrogation and appropriation are foundational postcolonial strategies (The Empire Writes Back); Ngugi wa Thiong'o's Weep Not, Child (1964) was the first published English novel by an East African writer; and Said, Bhabha, and Spivak are key postcolonial theorists. Statement (B) is false because postcolonial theory deconstructs colonial binaries, and (D) is false because Wide Sargasso Sea is set in the Caribbean (Jamaica and Dominica), not Africa.

items.title: Q40 · Dec 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Medieval & Middle English Literature · Unit II: Poetry · Thomas Aquinas, Dante Alighieri, Geoffrey Chaucer, Thomas Malory
items.stem: Indicate the correct chronological order of publication of the following literary works: (A) Beowulf (B) Divina Commedia (C) Summa Theologica (D) Le Morte d' Arthur (E) Canterbury Tales Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: The chronological order of composition and publication is: the Old English epic Beowulf (c. 8th-10th century), Thomas Aquinas's Summa Theologiae (c. 1265-1274), Dante's Divina Commedia (c. 1308-1320), Geoffrey Chaucer's The Canterbury Tales (c. 1387-1400), and Thomas Malory's Le Morte d'Arthur (1485) [(A), (C), (B), (E), (D)].

items.title: Q41 · Dec 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · Sri Aurobindo
items.stem: Chronologically arrange the following works of Sri Aurobindo in accordance with their year of publication: (A) The Hour of God (B) The Mother (C) The Life Divine (D) The Future Poetry (E) The Synthesis of Yoga Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Sri Aurobindo's works appeared in book publication in the following order: The Mother (1928), The Future Poetry (serialized 1917-1920, book 1953), The Life Divine (revised book edition 1939-1940), The Hour of God (compiled posthumously 1959), and The Synthesis of Yoga (complete book edition 1955/1971), corresponding to the sequence [(B), (D), (C), (A), (E)].

items.title: Q42 · Dec 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · E. M. Forster
items.stem: Which among the following are not mentioned as the aspects of the novel by E.M. Forster? (A) Story (B) Imagination (C) Plot (D) Harmony (E) Prophecy Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: In Aspects of the Novel (1927), E.M. Forster lists seven specific aspects of the novel: The Story, People, The Plot, Fantasy, Prophecy, Pattern, and Rhythm. Neither 'Imagination' (B) nor 'Harmony' (D) is included among Forster's seven aspects.

items.title: Q43 · Dec 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Postmodern & Contemporary Literature · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · R. K. Narayan, Bhabani Bhattacharya, Mulk Raj Anand, Manohar Malgonkar
items.stem: Match List - I with List - II. List - I (Novel) List II (Writer) (A) Waiting for the Mahatama (I) Bhabani Bhattacharya (B) So Many Hungers (II) R.K. Narayan (C) The Sword and the Sickle (III) Manohar Malgonkar (D) Distant Drum (IV) Mulk Raj Anand Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: The correct novel-to-author pairings are: R.K. Narayan wrote Waiting for the Mahatma (1955) [(A)-(II)]; Bhabani Bhattacharya wrote So Many Hungers! (1947) [(B)-(I)]; Mulk Raj Anand wrote The Sword and the Sickle (1942) [(C)-(IV)]; and Manohar Malgonkar wrote Distant Drum (1960) [(D)-(III)].

items.title: Q44 · Dec 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Literary Criticism & Theory · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post World War II · Gilles Deleuze, Felix Guattari
items.stem: What does aptly define minor literature, according to Giles Deleuze?
items.explanation: In Kafka: Toward a Minor Literature (1975), Gilles Deleuze and Félix Guattari identify the 'deterritorialization of language' as the first defining characteristic of a minor literature, where a minority uses a major language (such as Kafka using German in Prague) by subverting it from within.

items.title: Q45 · Dec 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · Dodie Smith, T. S. Eliot, Ford Madox Ford
items.stem: Which one of these is not a literary journal/magazine?
items.explanation: The Hundred and One Dalmatians is a 1956 children's novel by Dodie Smith, whereas The Egoist (1914-1919), The Criterion (edited by T.S. Eliot, 1922-1939), and The English Review (founded by Ford Madox Ford, 1908) were prominent modernist literary magazines.

items.title: Q46 · Dec 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Victorian Period · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Leo Tolstoy
items.stem: "All happy families are alike; every unhappy family is unhappy in its own way." It is the opening line of the novel:
items.explanation: This world-famous aphorism ('All happy families are alike; every unhappy family is unhappy in its own way') is the opening sentence of Leo Tolstoy's realist novel Anna Karenina (1878).

items.title: Q47 · Dec 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Literary Criticism & Theory · Unit I: Drama · Bharata Muni
items.stem: How many major forms of drama have been described by Bharata in his manual of dramaturgy?
items.explanation: In Chapter 18 of the Natyashastra, Bharata Muni classifies classical Indian drama into ten major dramatic forms (Dasa Rupaka): Nataka, Prakarana, Bhana, Prahasana, Dima, Vyayoga, Samavakara, Vithi, Anka, and Ihamriga.

items.title: Q48 · Dec 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Literary Criticism & Theory · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post World War II · Toni Morrison, Adrienne Rich
items.stem: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R). Assertion (A): Toni Morrison and Adrienne Rich have contributed to a distinctive style. Reason (R): Feminism, Adrienne Rich observes, is the field where "subjectivity and politics have to come together" in the most natural way. In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A).
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct.
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct.
items.explanation: Both statements are factually correct: Toni Morrison and Adrienne Rich each created a distinctive aesthetic style in American literature, and Adrienne Rich observed in her feminist essays that subjectivity and politics unite in feminism. However, Rich's theoretical comment on feminist methodology does not explain why both writers evolved their specific stylistic signatures, so Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).

items.title: Q49 · Dec 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Literary Criticism & Theory · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post World War II · Homi K. Bhabha
items.stem: Identify the correct option(s) in the theorisation of nation by Homi K. Bhabha. (A) Nation arises from similarities among people. (B) Nationalist representation is defined by ambivalence. (C) Nationalist representation engages with two contradictory modes of representation (D) Nationalist discourses are split by a disruptive double-narrative movement (E) Nation is a stable and fixed category Choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: In 'DissemiNation' (from Nation and Narration, 1990), Homi Bhabha argues that nationalist representation is inherently ambivalent (B), caught between two contradictory modes - the pedagogical and the performative (C), and split by a disruptive double-narrative movement (D). Statements (A) and (E) are false because Bhabha insists the nation is never fixed, stable, or founded on organic cultural uniformity.

items.title: Q50 · Dec 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Literary Criticism & Theory · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post World War II · Elaine Showalter
items.stem: The term 'Gynocriticism' refers to :
options: Production of writings on women by men
Production and analysis of writings by women on women
items.explanation: Coined by Elaine Showalter in 'Toward a Feminist Poetics' (1979), 'gynocriticism' defines the critical study of women as writers, focusing specifically on female literary history, themes, genres, and the production of writings by women on women.

items.title: Q51 · Dec 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Literary Criticism & Theory · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · Bharata Muni, Bhamaha, Anandavardhana, Kuntaka, Kshemendra
items.stem: Arrange the following texts chronologically: (A) Bharat's Natyashastra (B) Kshemendra's Aucityavicharacharcha (C) Bhamah's Kavyalankara (D) Kuntak's Vakroktijivitam (E) Anandavardhan's Dhvanyaloka Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: The historical sequence of these classical Sanskrit poetics treatises is: Bharata's Natyashastra (c. 2nd century BCE-2nd century CE), Bhamaha's Kavyalankara (c. 7th century CE), Anandavardhana's Dhvanyaloka (9th century CE), Kuntaka's Vakroktijivitam (late 10th-early 11th century CE), and Kshemendra's Aucityavicharacharcha (11th century CE) [(A), (C), (E), (D), (B)].

items.title: Q52 · Dec 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit V: Language: Basic Concepts, Theories and Pedagogy · Lewis Carroll
items.stem: A portmanteau is:
options: A word which sounds the same but have different meanings.
A word that results from blending two or more words or part of words.
Creation of new words without reference to the existing morphological resources.
Copying a word that originally belonged to one language into another language.
items.explanation: In linguistics, a portmanteau (blend word) is formed by fusing the sounds and meanings of two or more distinct words, such as 'smog' (smoke + fog) or 'motel' (motor + hotel), a term famously introduced by Lewis Carroll in Through the Looking-Glass (1871).

items.title: Q53 · Dec 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Literary Criticism & Theory · Unit I: Drama · Marjorie Boulton
items.stem: Who among the following described drama in the following words? "A true play is three dimensional; it is literature that walks and talks before our eyes."
items.explanation: British literary scholar Marjorie Boulton provided this definition of drama in Chapter 1 of her foundational guide The Anatomy of Drama (1960), underscoring that dramatic literature is created for living, three-dimensional physical realization on stage.

items.title: Q54 · Dec 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Victorian Period · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Leo Tolstoy
items.stem: What among the following is not true about Anna Karenina?
options: The novel is written in eight parts.
It tells the story of two major characters, Anna and Konstantin Levin.
The novel is revolutionary in its treatment of women.
items.explanation: Leo Tolstoy's Anna Karenina was serialized in The Russian Messenger between 1875 and 1877 and first appeared in complete book form in 1878, making the publication date of 1872 factually incorrect.

items.title: Q55 · Dec 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VI: English in India: History, Evolution and Futures
items.stem: Which among the following statement is not true about NEP-2020?
options: NEP-2020 recommends that there should be high quality learning and print material in Indian languages
The Policy recommends early implementation of three-language formulae to promote multilingualism
The Policy recommends that English language should be the only medium of instruction at elementary level
The Policy recommends teaching in local language wherever possible
items.explanation: India's National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 strongly advocates mother tongue, home language, or regional language as the medium of instruction up to at least Grade 5, explicitly refuting the idea of English being the sole medium of elementary instruction.

items.title: Q56 · Dec 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Literary Criticism & Theory · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post World War II · Michel Foucault, Jeremy Bentham
items.stem: 'Panopticism' is a concept that refers to external spying. Who among the following coined this term?
items.explanation: Michel Foucault developed the theoretical concept of 'Panopticism' in Discipline and Punish: The Birth of the Prison (1975), transforming Jeremy Bentham's 18th-century circular prison blueprint into a profound critique of modern institutional surveillance, power-knowledge, and self-policing subjects.

items.title: Q57 · Dec 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Victorian Period · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Gustave Flaubert, Joseph Conrad, Nadine Gordimer, R. K. Narayan

Narayan (D) "A Horse and Two Goats" (IV) Nadine Gordimer Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: The correct short story-to-author pairings are: Gustave Flaubert wrote 'A Simple Heart' (Un cœur simple, 1877) [(A)-(II)]; Joseph Conrad wrote the African colonial tale 'An Outpost of Progress' (1897) [(B)-(I)]; Nadine Gordimer wrote 'Six Feet of the Country' (1956) [(C)-(IV)]; and R.K. Narayan wrote 'A Horse and Two Goats' (1970) [(D)-(III)].

items.title: Q58 · Dec 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Literary Criticism & Theory · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post World War II · Sigmund Freud
items.stem: According to Sigmund Freud, civilisation is to some extent the cumulative product of our psychology. Choose the correct option(s): (A) The purpose of human life is the pursuit of happiness. (B) Man is wholly good. (C) Abolition of private property will remove ill-will and hostility among men. (D) Creative art reflects the purpose of human life. (E) Civilisation is analogous with the human psyche. Choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: In Civilization and Its Discontents (1930), Sigmund Freud argues that human beings strive after happiness under the pleasure principle (A), creative art offers sublimated satisfaction of instinctual desires (D), and the developmental trajectory of civilization parallels that of the individual psyche (E). Statements (B) and (C) are false because Freud posited an innate aggressive drive (Thanatos) and explicitly dismissed the communist belief that abolishing private property would eliminate human aggression.

items.title: Q59 · Dec 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Literary Criticism & Theory · Unit VII: Cultural Studies · Mikhail Bakhtin, Raymond Williams, William Empson, Michel Foucault
items.stem: Match List - I with List - II. List - I (Term) List - II (Coined by) (A) Heteroglossia (I) William Empson (B) Structures of Feeling (II) Raymond Williams (C) Ambiguity (III) Mikhail Bakhtin (D) Discourse (IV) Michel Foucault Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: The correct matches of theoretical concepts to their theorists are: Mikhail Bakhtin theorized 'heteroglossia' in 'Discourse in the Novel' [(A)-(III)]; Raymond Williams introduced 'structures of feeling' in The Long Revolution [(B)-(II)]; William Empson established 'ambiguity' in Seven Types of Ambiguity [(C)-(I)]; and Michel Foucault conceptualized 'discourse' in The Archaeology of Knowledge [(D)-(IV)].

items.title: Q60 · Dec 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Victorian Period · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Thomas Hardy
items.stem: Which of the following novels of Thomas Hardy was first published in an abridged form as Hearts Insurgent?
items.explanation: Thomas Hardy's final completed novel Jude the Obscure (1895) was originally serialized in an abridged, censored format in Harper's New Monthly Magazine between December 1894 and November 1895 under the title Hearts Insurgent (initially announced as The Simpletons).

items.title: Q61 · Dec 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Renaissance, Elizabethan & Jacobean Age · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · Francis Bacon
items.stem: Which work of Francis Bacon explains the new logic or inductive method of reasoning?
items.explanation: Francis Bacon's philosophical treatise Novum Organum Scientiarum (1620, meaning 'New Instrument of Science') expounded the new inductive logic and empirical observation, aiming to replace the traditional deductive syllogistic system of Aristotle's Organon.

items.title: Q62 · Dec 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Literary Criticism & Theory · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post World War II · Homi K. Bhabha
items.stem: Match List - I with List - II. List I (Term) List - II (Definition) (A) Ambivalence (I) Rejection of a normative concept of 'correct' or 'standard' English (B) Magic Realism (II) Marriage or cohabitation by persons of different race (C) Abrogation (III) Complex mix of attraction and repulsion (D) Miscegenation (IV) Inclusion of fantastic or mythical elements into seemingly realistic fiction Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: The correct critical definitions are: Ambivalence is the simultaneous attraction and repulsion marking colonial discourse [(A)-(III)]; Magic Realism weaves fantastical or mythical events into realistic narratives [(B)-(IV)]; Abrogation is the postcolonial rejection of imperial standard English and metropolitan linguistic norms [(C)-(I)]; and Miscegenation refers to interracial sexual relations or marriage [(D)-(II)].

items.title: Q63 · Dec 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Romantic Period · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Jane Austen
items.stem: Which among the following is not a character from Jane Austen's novel Persuasion?
items.explanation: Mary Crawford is a fashionable, worldly character in Jane Austen's Mansfield Park (1814), whereas Sir Walter Elliot, Lady Russell, and Captain Frederick Wentworth are central characters in Persuasion (1818).

items.title: Q64 · Dec 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Romantic Period · Unit II: Poetry · William Blake
items.stem: Name the poet who has composed the following poems: (a) The Divine Image (b) The Holy Thursday (c) The Little Boy Lost (d) The Little Boy Found
items.explanation: All four poems were written and engraved by William Blake: 'The Divine Image', 'Holy Thursday', 'The Little Boy Lost', and 'The Little Boy Found' belong to his illuminated masterwork Songs of Innocence (1789), paired with companion poems in Songs of Experience (1794).

items.title: Q65 · Dec 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Romantic Period · Unit II: Poetry · John Keats
items.stem: According to Greek Mythology, who is a Psyche in John Keats' "Ode to Psyche"?
items.explanation: In Classical mythology (narrated in Apuleius' The Golden Ass), Psyche was a mortal princess of exquisite beauty who endured trials imposed by Venus before marrying Cupid and being granted immortality, as Keats highlights when addressing her as the youngest divinity of Olympus in 'Ode to Psyche' (1819).

items.title: Q66 · Dec 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Literary Criticism & Theory · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem: Match List I with List II. List - I (Literary Device) List - II (Definition) (A) Hyperbole (I) Referring to something by the name of something else that is closely connected with it (B) Metonymy (II) A roundabout or indirect manner of writing or speaking (C) Synecdoche (III) A figure of speech in which a part represents the whole (D) Periphrasis (IV) An intentional exaggeration for emphasis or comic effect Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: The correct rhetorical device definitions are: Hyperbole is deliberate exaggeration for dramatic or comedic emphasis [(A)-(IV)]; Metonymy names an entity through a closely related associate or attribute [(B)-(I)]; Synecdoche uses a part to signify the whole (or whole for part) [(C)-(III)]; and Periphrasis (circumlocution) uses roundabout language instead of concise phrasing [(D)-(II)].

items.title: Q67 · Dec 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Postmodern & Contemporary Literature · Unit IV: Non-Fictional Prose · Deepti Naval, Andre Agassi, Mary Kom, Sachin Tendulkar
items.stem: Which among the following is not written by a sportsperson?
options: Playing It My Way: My Autobiography
A Country Called Childhood: A Memoir
items.explanation: A Country Called Childhood: A Memoir (2022) was written by acclaimed Indian actress, poet, and painter Deepti Naval, whereas Open (2009) is by tennis star Andre Agassi, Unbreakable (2013) is by boxer Mary Kom, and Playing It My Way (2014) is by cricketer Sachin Tendulkar.

items.title: Q68 · Dec 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Literary Criticism & Theory · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post World War II · Frantz Fanon, Homi K. Bhabha, Edward Said, Benedict Anderson
items.stem: Match List - I with List - II. List - I (Work) List - II (Author) (A) The Wretched of the Earth (I) Benedict Anderson (B) Nation and Narration (II) Homi K. Bhabha (C) Culture and Imperialism (III) Edward W. Said (D) Imagined Communities (IV) Frantz Fanon Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: The correct seminal theoretical matches are: Frantz Fanon authored The Wretched of the Earth (1961) [(A)-(IV)]; Homi K. Bhabha edited Nation and Narration (1990) [(B)-(II)]; Edward W. Said wrote Culture and Imperialism (1993) [(C)-(III)]; and Benedict Anderson wrote Imagined Communities: Reflections on the Origin and Spread of Nationalism (1983) [(D)-(I)].

items.title: Q69 · Dec 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · D. H. Lawrence
items.stem: What is not true about D.H. Lawrence's Sons and Lovers? (A) Sons and Lovers is a semi-autobiographical novel. (B) It is a psychological study of the familial and love relationships of a working-class English family. (C) The film adaptation of the novel was directed by Jack Cardiff. (D) The storyline traces three generations of Brangwen family. (E) The novel narrates the story of Paul Morel whose love for his beloved overshadows the affectionate bond with his mother. Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Statements (D) and (E) are not true of D.H. Lawrence's Sons and Lovers (1913): the multi-generational chronicle of the Brangwen family is the subject of The Rainbow (1915), and Paul Morel's consuming Oedipal attachment to his mother Gertrude Morel cripples his relationships with Miriam Leivers and Clara Dawes, rather than his lovers overshadowing his mother.

items.title: Q70 · Dec 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Romantic Period · Unit II: Poetry · Percy Bysshe Shelley, Lord Byron
items.stem: Which among the following poems has not been composed by P.B. Shelley?
items.explanation: 'When We Two Parted' (1816) is a celebrated lyric poem of secret heartbreak written by Lord Byron, whereas 'To Wordsworth', 'Mutability', and 'Hymn to Intellectual Beauty' are well-known Romantic poems by Percy Bysshe Shelley.

items.title: Q71 · Dec 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Literary Criticism & Theory · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post World War II · Michel Foucault
items.stem: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R). Assertion (A): Discourses are cultural and social practices rooted in psychic and physical reality. Reason (R): Foucault defines discourse as the material manifestation of thought which shapes our subjectivity. In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A).
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct.
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct.
items.explanation: In Michel Foucault's archaeology and genealogy, discourses are not mere abstract linguistic constructs but embodied, material practices governed by historical rules that construct and discipline social reality and human subjectivity, making Reason (R) the precise theoretical foundation and explanation for Assertion (A).

items.title: Q72 · Dec 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Postmodern & Contemporary Literature · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · V. S. Naipaul, Salman Rushdie, Chitra Banerjee Divakaruni, Bharati Mukherjee, Anand Giridharadas
items.stem: Arrange the following in the chronological order of the date/year of publication: (A) Chitra Banerjee Divakaruni's The Mistress of Spices (B) Anand Giridhar Das's India Calling: An Intimate Portrait of a Nation's Remaking (C) V.S. Naipaul's India: A Wounded Civilisation (D) Bharati Mukherjee's Desirable Daughters (E) Salman Rushdie's Midnight's Children Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: The chronological sequence of publication is: V.S. Naipaul's India: A Wounded Civilization (1977), Salman Rushdie's Midnight's Children (1981), Chitra Banerjee Divakaruni's The Mistress of Spices (1997), Bharati Mukherjee's Desirable Daughters (2002), and Anand Giridharadas's India Calling (2011) [(C), (E), (A), (D), (B)].

items.title: Q73 · Dec 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit I: Drama · Arthur Miller
items.stem: Which of the following is true about Arthur Miller's plays? (A) After the Fall is a semi-autobiographical play. (B) Incident of Vichy deals with Nazi prosecution of the Jews. (C) The Price anticipates economic crash. (D) The Creation of the World is not a serio-comic re-writing of the story of Jesus. (E) The Crucible uses a specific setting to consider the responsibilities of the artist. Choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Arthur Miller's After the Fall (1964) is an intensely reflective semi-autobiographical drama dramatizing his marriage to Marilyn Monroe and his confrontation with the Red Scare (A), while Incident at Vichy (1964) confronts the Nazi detention, interrogation, and racial persecution of Jews in occupied France (B).

items.title: Q74 · Dec 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Literary Criticism & Theory · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post World War II · Julia Kristeva
items.stem: Identify the correct option in Julia Kristeva's definition of 'chora': (A) Liminal Space (B) Space of the marginalised (C) Non-expressive totality created by the bodily drives (D) The chora has no fixed identity (E) It precedes the linguistic sign Choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: In Revolution in Poetic Language (1974), Julia Kristeva adopts Plato's concept of the 'chora' to designate the pre-Oedipal semiotic realm: a dynamic, non-expressive totality produced by instinctual bodily drives (C) that lacks unified or fixed spatial identity (D) and precedes the symbolic linguistic sign and syntax (E).

items.title: Q75 · Dec 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Literary Criticism & Theory · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post World War II · Edward Said
items.stem: "Being a white man, in short, was a very concrete manner of being-in-the-world, a way of taking hold of reality, language and thought." What does the theorist signify by the term 'white man' here?
items.explanation: In Orientalism (1978), Edward Said explains that being a 'white man' in the colonial empire was not simply a racial categorization, but an institutionalized epistemological posture and an authoritative vantage point of imperial governance and mastery - signifying a form of colonial authority.

items.title: Q76 · Dec 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Victorian Period · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Fyodor Dostoevsky
items.stem: "I am a sick man... I am a spiteful man. I am an unattractive man. I think my liver is diseased." These are the opening lines of:
options: Gabriel Garcia Marquez's Love in the Time of Cholera
Daniel Defoe's A Journal of the Plague Year
items.explanation: These famously cynical and self-lacerating lines open Fyodor Dostoevsky's groundbreaking existentialist novella Notes from Underground (1864), spoken by the unnamed Underground Man in Saint Petersburg.

items.title: Q77 · Dec 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Literary Criticism & Theory · Unit VII: Cultural Studies · Stanley Fish, Jonathan Dollimore, Alan Sinfield, Raymond Williams
items.stem: Who among the following is not associated with Cultural Imperialism?
items.explanation: Stanley Fish is a prominent American reader-response theorist known for his concepts of the 'informed reader' and 'interpretive communities', whereas cultural materialists and cultural studies scholars like Jonathan Dollimore, Alan Sinfield, and Raymond Williams directly investigated cultural imperialism, hegemony, and political ideology.

items.title: Q78 · Dec 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Victorian Period · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · John Campbell Shairp, William Shakespeare
items.stem: "Did not Shakespeare hate and despise Iago and Edmund?" Identify the book in which this question has been mentioned.
items.explanation: This rhetorical inquiry into Shakespeare's moral perspective towards his greatest tragic villains (Iago from Othello and Edmund from King Lear) is posed in Scottish literary critic and Oxford Professor of Poetry John Campbell Shairp's scholarly work Aspects of Poetry (1881).

items.title: Q79 · Dec 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Postmodern & Contemporary Literature · Unit III: Fiction & Short Story · Sharankumar Limbale
items.stem: Choose the correct option(s) in the New Historicist reading of Dalit writing: (A) Dalit writing does not essentialise Indian society, culture and identity. Read the following stanza and answer the questions that follow:

"Shall I compare thee to a Summer's Day?
Thou art more lovely and more temperate:
Rough winds do shake the darling buds of May,
And summer's lease hath all too short a date.
Sometimes too hot the eye of heaven shines,
And often is his gold complexion dimm'd."

Question:
Which of the following statements rightly shows the relationship of upameya with upamana in the poem:
options: Both upamana and upameya are equal
Both are governed by position and superimposition
items.explanation: In classical Sanskrit poetics (Alankara Shastra), the upameya is the subject of comparison (the beloved Fair Youth) and the upamana is the standard of comparison (the Summer's Day); in lines 1-2 ('Thou art more lovely and more temperate'), the speaker asserts the beloved's superiority over the summer's day, making the upameya superior to the upamana (Vyatireka alankara).

Question:
The poem is an example of:
options: Parampariterupaka (consequential metaphor) because here the superimposition, undermined by a resemblance, is the cause of another superimposition.
Nirangarupaka (entire metaphor) because here upameya is superimposed by upamana together with its subordinate parts.
Malarupaka (deficient metaphorserial) because here upameya is superimposed by serial of upamanas.
Mishritarupaka (mixed metaphor) because here the common attribute, the words implying comparison, upamana and upameya, all are expressed.
items.explanation: The stanza exemplifies Paramparitarupaka (consequential or linked metaphor) in Indian poetics because the initial metaphorical superimposition comparing the youth to a summer's day establishes the causal basis for the subsequent superimpositions concerning his unfading, eternal summer and verse.

items.title: Q96 · Dec 2023 (Shift 1)
items.meta: Modernist & Early 20th Century · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism · William Empson
items.stem:
[Reading Comprehension: Prose Passage]
Read the following passage and answer the questions that follow:

"Some sort of parallel may be found in the way logical connectives are usually unnecessary and often misleading, because too simple. Omitting an adjective one would need 'therefore' stressing the adjective 'although'; both logical connections are implied if the sentences are just put after another. In the same way, people are accustomed to judge automatically the forces that hold together a variety of ideas; they feel they know about the forces, if they have analysed the ideas; many forces, indeed, are covertly included within ideas; and so of the two elements, each of which defines the other, it is much easier to find words for the ideas than for the forces. Most of the ambiguities I have considered here seem to me beautiful; I consider, then, that I have shown by example, in showing the nature of the ambiguity, the nature of the forces which are adequate to hold it together. It would seem very artificial to do it the other way round, and very tedious to do it both ways at once. I wish only, then, to say here that such vaguely imagined 'forces' are essential to the totality of a poem and they cannot be discussed in terms of ambiguity, because they are complementary to it. But by discussing 'ambiguity', a great deal may be made clear about them. In particular, if there is contradiction, the greater the tension; in some way other than by the contradiction, the tension must be conveyed, and must be sustained."

Question:
What does the term "logical connectives" mean?
options: The statement of logical form in addition to logical context
items.explanation: In this excerpt from Seven Types of Ambiguity (1930), William Empson equates logical connectives (such as 'therefore' and 'although') with explicit statements of logical form, arguing that they are often clumsy in poetry where juxtaposition alone conveys complex logical relations.
